source.title: Information Capacity of Generative Video Compression: Quantifying the Rate-Compute Exchange at Identical Quality
source.authors: Cheng Yuan; Jia-Wei Shao; Xue-Long Li

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Applies a two-factor power-law form to generative video compression and reports measured fit results in a video setting, rather than testing language-model pretraining loss scaling.
record.gate_note: The study tests a power-law distortion surface for video compression against measured data. It does not test language-model loss scaling, small-run extrapolation, parameter/token allocation, architecture sensitivity, or downstream-task predictability. Its citations to language-model scaling laws are background, not results.
record.test_reason: The paper borrows the compute–loss power-law form as a modelling tool. It fits the perceptual distortion (DISTS) of two fixed, already-trained video decoders against transmission bitrate and inference-time denoising compute. That is not loss falling with parameters, tokens or training compute, so it does not test V5 or any other version. The rate axis also spans only a factor of 1.2–2, not orders of magnitude. The 1.3B-vs-14B contrast is two systems that also differ in GOP length and side information, not a size sweep.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that the two-factor power law fits DISTS within a few percent, and that the 14B decoder converts compute into rate savings about ten times more efficiently than the 1.3B decoder (median factor 9). They also conclude that the exchange rate varies strongly across the operating plane and across datasets.
record.recipe_differences: The paper borrows the functional form of compute–loss scaling but fits video reconstruction DISTS against transmission rate and decoder inference compute, rather than language-model pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or training compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted exponents and derived information capacity vary across datasets and between the two decoder sizes; the paper reports DISTS alone and uses theoretical DiT FLOPs as compute.

fits_no_version.finding: For two fixed generative video decoders on five datasets, an additive two-factor power law with a floor fits DISTS as a function of bitrate and inference denoising compute. The mean relative error is 0.4–2.7% and the maximum error is below 7.1% over 760 configurations. Rate ranges span only a factor of 1.2–2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inference-time quality of generative codecs follows a power law in transmitted rate and decoder sampling compute.

record.problems: Evidence is limited to two existing GVC systems, five datasets, and DISTS; reported triples are dataset means, with no uncertainty intervals stated. Compute is theoretical DiT FLOPs and excludes memory-bound execution, latency, and energy. The authors also note that results may differ for other quality metrics.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out. The paper separately reports information-capacity values and rate savings, but these are derived rate–decoder-compute results rather than direct measurements of the power-law form named by V5.

untested.parts: No language-model pretraining loss or parameter/token/compute sweep.
No extrapolation from small runs to larger runs.
No compute-optimal allocation between parameters and tokens.
No comparison of shape at a fixed parameter count.
No training-scale sweep (parameters, data or training compute) for video or other modalities. Only inference-time rate and step sweeps on fixed models.
No comparison of fitting choices for language-model scaling laws.

record.verdict_notes: The record's reader linked all rows to V5 and labelled them 'supports'. That is wrong: V5 concerns power-law scaling of loss with training scale in other modalities, whereas this study fits an inference-time rate/sampling-step distortion surface on fixed trained models. The scaling-law citations [9,10] serve only as motivation for the functional form. Preprint, no uncertainty intervals.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out language-model pretraining loss or parameter, token, or training-compute sweep.
No small-run fit used to predict substantially larger language-model runs.
No fixed training-compute budget or loss-minimising parameter/token allocation is studied.
No comparison of language-model depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.

Tests a rate–decoder-compute power law for video compression using DISTS; does not test image models, repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer, or other training regimes, and does not establish the form for other quality metrics.

Does not test language-model scaling-law exponents, compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, alternative fitting choices for those laws, or whether language-model curves bend away from a power law.
